t: for the verse converted it into a positive commandment, that if he robbed he must return. The negative commandment ("you shall not rob") was converted into a positive commandment ("and he shall return the robbed item"), and one does not receive lashes for such a negative commandment (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).

and even if he burned the robbed item he does not receive lashes, etc.. Although for a negative commandment converted into a positive one, if he did not fulfill the positive commandment he receives lashes, and he should have received lashes since he did not return the robbed item, he is nonetheless exempt from lashes for another reason: since he must pay the value of the robbed item, and no negative commandment that carries a payment obligation incurs lashes (there, and see also Hilchot Genevah 1:1).
and it is forbidden to rob anything by Torah law. By the Torah it is forbidden to rob even less than the value of a perutah (except that there is no obligation to return it, as below 5:6).
even a gentile who serves idolatry it is forbidden to rob. See also Hilchot Genevah 1:1.
for example, that he snatched movable property from his hand. And with robbing land too he transgresses a negative commandment (Hilchot Genevah 7:11).
or that he overpowered his slaves and his animals. Seized them by force.
and used them. See below 3:6-7.
or that he went down into his field and ate its fruit. See below 9:5.
with the owners' consent. Unlike robbery, where the item came into his hand without the owners' consent.
for example, he had a loan or a deposit in his fellow's hand. That he lent to his fellow or deposited with him.

or wages. It seems this means that his fellow worked for him as a hired worker and he holds his wages in his hand and does not give them to him. And although in this case the fellow did not give him money, it is still included in the prohibition of oppression (see Sefer HaMitzvot, Negative Commandment 238, Hilchot Sechirut 11:2).
violent and hard. A violent person with whom it is hard to litigate.

the Sages enacted for the sake of the repentant that he give its value and not lose the building. They made an enactment to ease matters for robbers who wish to repent, since if returning the robbed item itself would cause a loss, it would make it hard for robbers to return to the right path (and see below halachah 13 and below 2:2 for further enactments to ease matters for the repentant).
and made it into the roof of a sukkah for the festival. He built it into the sukkah of the festival of Sukkot (see also Hilchot Sukkah 5:25).

he gives him its value. Since he fulfills a commandment with it, it is treated as a permanent building into which the enactment for the repentant applies on the festival, even though in itself it is not a permanent structure (Rashi and Meiri, Sukkah 31a).
but after the festival. If he claimed it from him after Sukkot.
and did not build it with mortar. For if he joined it with mortar it is judged a permanent structure and has the law of a beam built into a building (Rashi there).
it changed, he pays its value. As explained below chapter 2.

he must pay only the principal. Unlike a thief, who pays a fine if there are witnesses that he stole (Hilchot Genevah 1:4-6). And if he swore falsely and then admitted, he pays principal plus a fifth and brings a guilt offering (below 7:1-2).
and built it into the palace. Made it part of the palace, which is a large building.
since it did not change. Although now it is part of the building, nonetheless in itself it remains as it was.
even though he transgressed. The Torah prohibition of robbery.
it is not in the category of returning a robbed item. There is no commandment to return the robbed item.
bundles. Of vegetables and the like.
and the three of them are together worth two perutot and he returned two to him. So it turns out that he now holds a bundle worth less than a perutah.

there is robbery here but no commandment to return a robbed item here. He robbed the value of a perutah and became obligated to return it, but since less than a perutah of what he robbed remains in his hand, he is not obligated by the commandment of returning (the version before us in the Talmud, Bava Kamma 105a, reads: "there is no robbery here, and there is no commandment to return a robbed item here," and the Rishonim there brought several explanations; see the commentators who discussed the relationship between Maimonides' words here and this version).
in a settled place. An inhabited place.
lest it be seized from me here. For the wilderness is a place of danger and the robbed item is not safe with him.

and likewise with the value of the robbed item. In a case where he pays its value, the choice is the victim's not to receive the payment in the wilderness (see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 13:8, Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 7:11).
and slipped it to him in the account. When he settled accounts with the victim about another matter, he added the value of the robbed item into the account without his knowledge.

for a person tends to feel his purse at all times, etc.. A person is accustomed to check often how much money he has in his wallet, and one can assume that he already counted the coins that returned to him together with the other coins he had in his wallet.

and a count without knowledge discharges. Although the robber did not inform the owner that he had returned the money to his wallet, since the owner now knows that he has all his money, the robber is released from responsibility (compare Hilchot Genevah 4:10-11).

and if he returned it to a purse with nothing in it, he has not discharged. For he does not usually feel it at all times, and since he does not know that there is now money in it, he will not be careful to guard it.
and pressed him with friends and urged him until he took it from him. He sent his friends to persuade him to sell it to him until he finally agreed.
and one does not receive lashes for this negative commandment, for it involves no act. Since the prohibition is the urging of his fellow, and speech is not an act (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1).

and he does not transgress this negative commandment until he takes the item he coveted. For although the essence of the prohibition of coveting is the urging, one does not transgress the prohibition if the coveting did not reach the stage of an act of actually acquiring the item.

once he thought in his heart how he might buy this thing from him and his heart was enticed by it, he transgressed a negative commandment. This speaks of one who thought how to obtain his desire, but mere desire alone is not included in the prohibition (see Eight Chapters of Maimonides, chapter 6).
and desire is only in the heart alone. Desire in itself is a mental act and not a practical one.
even though he offered them much money. That he offered them a high payment.

from the deed of Ahab and Naboth. Ahab, king of Israel, coveted the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, and when Naboth would not agree to sell it to him, Ahab and Jezebel arranged to have him killed so that Ahab would receive the vineyard (I Kings, chapter 21).
"so are the ways of everyone greedy for gain; it takes away the life of its owners". Anyone who robs his fellow takes his life, even if only the value of a perutah.
it is an enactment of the Sages that they do not accept from him. One should not take the value of the robbed item from him.
in order to bring the upright path closer for the repentant. To ease matters for one who wants to return to the upright path (see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 4:5).

and even if the robber died and it is in the hands of his sons, it returns to its owners in kind. And this is not considered a change of possession that acquires together with despair (below 5:3). As for the obligation of the sons of a robber who died to return when the robbed item no longer exists, see below 5:5-6.
he acquired it by the change. And he does not need to return the robbed item itself, but pays the victim its value.
and pays its value as at the time of the robbery. According to what it was worth when it was robbed.
by oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
the robber acquired all the improvement that it improved after despair. As explained below 5:6.
rabbinically, for the sake of the repentant. The Sages enacted that the robber acquire the improvement after despair in order to make it easier for him to return the robbed item.
the buyer acquired it through despair and change of possession. And the same law applies to a thief (see Hilchot Genevah 5:3).

one who robs and improves and sells or bequeaths before despair, etc.. The robber himself acquires only the improvement after despair, but if he sold or bequeathed the robbed item, the buyer or heir acquires the improvement even without despair, and this is an enactment of the Sages (see Bava Kamma 96a).

and the victim returns and takes the value of the improvement from the robber, for he had not despaired. Between the robber and the victim the law remains that he does not acquire improvement made before despair, and therefore the victim collects from the robber the value of the improvement that he paid to the heir or buyer.

and likewise if the buyer or heir improved it, etc.. When the buyer or heir themselves improved the robbed item, they acquire the improvement even if the owners had not despaired, and the victim collects the improvement from the robber.
even if the gentile improved it, it returns to its owners. And he does not pay the gentile for improvement, for the gentile is not included in this enactment (Bava Kamma 96a).

the gentile sold it to a Jew after improving it... and if the victim seized it, we do not take it from his hand. This case was not decided in the Gemara (there), and because of the doubt we do not take money from one who holds it. But if the victim seized the improvement we do not take it from him, since he is now the one in possession.
we have already explained. Above halachot 1-2, and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:11-12.
and it grew. It grew wool.
he pays as at the time of the robbery. He returns the robbed item and the victim pays him for the improvement.
he pays the value of a cow about to give birth and the value of a ewe about to be sheared. And he acquired the offspring and the fleece because they came after despair.

it is still in its owners' possession even though the robber is liable for its accidents. Although the robber is liable for every accident and bears full responsibility like an owner, he does not have the law of an owner.
and consecrated. The animal as an offering.

and slaughtered after the owners despaired. After the consecration the owners despaired and then he slaughtered the animal outside the Temple (Mirkevet HaMishneh, which resolves the Raavad's objection in his critical notes).

it is in the robber's possession only from the moment he consecrated it, etc.. In Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot (18:14) it is explained that if he stole or robbed an animal and consecrated it and after despair slaughtered it outside, he is liable to karet like one who slaughters sacred offerings outside. And although it is not possible to consecrate something that is not one's own before despair, it is explained there that the Sages placed it in his possession in order to be strict with him so that he is liable to karet for slaughtering sacred offerings outside. And here it is explained that placing the animal in the robber's possession is from the time of the consecration onward and not already from the time of the robbery, so that he not gain the improvement from then (Mirkevet HaMishneh and Yad Peshutah).

if it was lean and he fattened it, even before despair he takes from the victim the improvement of the fattening. Some explained that this law too is for the sake of the repentant, that for improvement on which he spent money they enacted that he acquire it even before despair (Or Sameach and others; and see Even HaEzel, Nizkei Mamon 7:12, who explained differently; and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:11).
to its original state. To its initial state before it changed.
they return to being boards. They return to being wooden boards.
he must grind. Crumble.
a tongue. A raw piece.
he must return it to being a tongue. He must return it to being a tongue.
and planed them. Smoothed and polished them.
or dug in them. Carved in them to make them into containers or to carve another part of the vessel.
he beat it. Struck its fibers to separate them.
and whitened it. Cleaned it.
spun. Spun threads ready for weaving a garment.
and made it dust. Crumbled it.
and polished them and renewed them. Smoothed their surface and cleaned them.
they become dull. They become covered with a dark layer.
he robbed an attached palm tree and cut it down, he did not acquire it. Since its name was and remained a palm tree (Bava Kamma 96a).

he cut it into sections and made it into beams, he acquired. For this is a complete change, but if he merely cut it down and chopped it into sections and did not make beams of them, he did not acquire, because these are sections of a palm tree and not something else entirely (there).
if he cut them into boards until their name changed, he acquired. If he cut the beam into planks, this is a complete change.
he robbed leaves and made them into broom. He split the palm leaves into two parts in each leaf and made it into a sort of broom (Rashi, Bava Kamma 96a).
he robbed a lamb and it became a ram. He robbed a small lamb and kept it until it grew up and became a ram.
this is a change in his possession and he acquired it. Although he did not do an act with his hands, a substantive change occurred in the robbed item and he acquired it.
he robbed a vessel and broke it, we do not assess for him the depreciation. He cannot return the broken vessel and pay only the loss in value of the vessel according to the assessors' estimate.

for this is an enactment for the owners. And therefore although the vessel was broken or depreciated and a change was made in it, the robber did not acquire the item (and see the Gra, section 354 subsection 13, and Ketzot HaChoshen there subsection 3, who found difficulty in this; and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:15).
and became more expensive. It rose in price.

but the improvement of the price rise, if the robbed item exists, returns in kind. As for acquiring the improvement of the price rise when the robbed item no longer exists, see the beginning of the next chapter.
and it became more expensive with him and stood at four. It rose in price without any change occurring in it and its price stood at four dinars.

if he broke the jar, etc.. In principle the robber pays for the robbed item according to its value at the time of the robbery (Mishnah Bava Kamma 9:1), but when he destroyed it with his hands he pays according to its value at that time (see Bava Metzia 43a).
a wrapper. A covering, like a bag or box, made of palm leaves and the like, in which fresh dates are sold (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 16:5).
and when he sells them one by one he sells for ten. If he sells the dates separately he will receive ten coins for them.
and the victim cannot say to him, I would have sold them one by one. And therefore the value of the robbed item is ten.
and the same law applies to one who damages. Also in a case where he damaged his fellow's property we assess the damage in the same way.

and likewise anything similar to this with ordinary property, but with consecrated property it is not so, rather he pays ten. For an ordinary person the Sages were lenient to assess by the overall value, since we find that the Torah was lenient in a similar matter in monetary damages (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 4:13 and the explanation there), but with consecrated property they were not lenient (see Bava Metzia 99b).
it grew lean. It became thin, weakened.
for example, illnesses that have no cure. That have no remedies that would help them.
or the king invalidated it. Who decreed that the coin could not be used for payment.
this is like one who robbed a vessel and broke it, etc.. And the robber takes the robbed item and pays the victim its full value (see above 2:15).
and it is accepted in another country. It can be used for payment in another place.
or terumah and it became impure. And it is forbidden to eat.
chametz and Pesach passed over it. And it became forbidden for eating and benefit.
an animal on which a transgression was committed. For example, it was mated with by a person and was disqualified from being offered.
or that was disqualified from being offered. For example, a blemish developed in it.
or that was going out to be stoned. And it is forbidden for benefit, such as an ox that killed a person.
he must return its value as at the time of the robbery. And not according to its value when it was lost, as explained above 5:2.

therefore, etc.. Since he must pay if it is lost, it turns out it still has value even though it is forbidden for benefit, and therefore if he denied the robbery and swore about it, he must pay its value plus a fifth and a guilt offering (as below 7:1).
even though he transgressed a negative commandment. Of robbery (above 1:3).

we penalize him, even outside the Land. Although ordinarily judges outside the Land do not judge fines and do not even collect fines enacted by the Sages (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8-9), in exceptional cases it is permitted to act by emergency measure outside the ordinary law and to penalize one who breaks through the fences of religion or behaves violently (see there 24:6).
and we assess the wages or the improvement that he improved in the animal. We estimate how much the robber gained or how much his property improved because of the work.
the one who seizes. Holds by force.
he is exempt, for a person is pleased that his slave not be idle. Even though the slave becomes thin from the work, the slave's owner prefers this to an idle slave (Bava Kamma 97a).
if it is not made for hire. If the owner is not accustomed to rent it out.

if he went down to it in the manner of renting, etc.. That he intended to pay rent. In this case he can be judged as a renter who must pay rent, or as a robber (like one who borrows without knowledge, below halachah 15) who pays the depreciation, and therefore the owner of the ship will choose what to collect from him.
even though this resident is accustomed to rent a place for himself. That the resident is accustomed to rent a place for himself to live in.
for this one benefits and this one does not lose. The owners do not lose because of the resident's benefit, and therefore he does not have to pay them.
even though this one is not accustomed to rent. And it turns out that the resident does not gain by not paying rent for the courtyard.
and soaked dyes. Dyeing materials soaked in water separately from the wool.

he pays him the value of what he lost in the wool, etc.. When they assess the value of the dyed wool that the robber returns to the victim, the robber is at a disadvantage: if the value of the dyed wool decreased because of the dyeing he pays the difference, since he damaged the wool; and if the wool improved because of the dyes on it, he does not pay for what it improved (see Mirkevet HaMishneh).

and if the injured party seized the value of what was lacking from the dyes, we do not take it from his hand. For besides returning the wool, the robber must return the dyes. But there is a doubt about this whether returning the dyed wool is also considered returning the dye he took, or not. Therefore the court does not obligate him to pay for the dye, but if the owner seized the value of the dye from the dyer's property, we do not take it from his hand.
one who lays a hand on a deposit. He took the deposit that was deposited with him in order to bring it into his possession as a robber.

by means of his son, his slave and his agent, he is a robber and is liable for its accidents. Although ordinarily there is no agent for a transgression, with laying a hand the Sages learned that the agent's act binds the one who sent him (Kiddushin 42b).
he is not liable for its responsibility. As a robber; rather his law is still that of a guardian.
but he took the deposit... in order to lay a hand on it. That he brought it into his possession as a robber.
he became liable for its accidents. Of the jar and all the wine in it, since he lifted the whole jar.
the purse. A wallet.
and anything like a purse of things that are not one body. A container with several separate things in it that he lifted and intends to take only one thing from it.
this is a doubt. Perhaps only with a jar is he liable for all the wine because all the wine is one unit, and not in lifting a purse in which each dinar stands by itself.
it is in its owners' possession. And its law remains that of a deposit.
for he did not lift the jar. And the jar did not pass into his responsibility.

and if it turned sour he pays the value of all of it. If the wine remaining in the jar turned sour he is liable, since removing the revi'it of wine can cause the rest to turn sour (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 3:12).
and one of them took it and used it. One person took the item from them and used it.
until he returns it to the owners. And it is not enough that he return it to the one he took it from.

one who seizes a pledge from the hand of the borrower without the court's authorization. But a court agent is permitted to take the pledge by force from the borrower, provided he does not enter his house (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 3:4).

the Sages imposed a fine on robbers, etc.. And the reason for the fine is "so that damages and lawlessness among people do not multiply" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 7:3, and compare Hilchot Chovel u-Mazik 5:4).
one who entered his fellow's house to take a pledge. And it is known that he entered for this purpose, and since it is forbidden to take a pledge by force he is treated as a robber (above 3:16).
under his wings. Under the wings of his garment.

the homeowner swears while holding an object. While holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8, and see there halachah 11), according to the law of those who swear and take (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:2).
where he claimed things that he is presumed to have. That it is plausible that the claimant had such things in his possession.
for it is presumed that such things as he claimed are deposited with him. That it is plausible that such things are given to him for safekeeping.

even if he said, "I never entered," since he contradicts the witnesses, he is exempt. Although it was shown by the witnesses that he lied about his entering the house, he is not established as a liar regarding his claim that he did not take vessels from the house.
he swears the heset oath. A light oath (without holding an object) that the Sages imposed on a defendant in cases where he is exempt from a severe oath (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:3).

for it is possible that he entered to rob and did not rob. And therefore the fact that he entered to take a pledge does not testify that he actually took vessels from his house, and they did not enact that the claimant swear and take.
there was one witness testifying that he entered. For example, he testifies that he entered to take a pledge (Maggid Mishneh), which is forbidden as robbery (see above 3:16).
since the witness does not know what was under his wings. For if he had known, he would have obligated him to take the Torah oath (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:1).

for he is not established as a robber except by two witnesses. Since the Sages' enactment that he swears and takes when it is not known how much he took is based on his having been established as a robber, if there is only one witness that he took, he was not established as a robber, and the claimant does not swear and take.
just as the homeowner swears and takes. When there are witnesses that he robbed and it is not known what he took.

so too the homeowner's guardian. Who guards for the homeowner. And his law is not that of a witness but of the homeowner himself, and after he swears how much he took, the homeowner collects from the robber.

even the guardian's wife. For the deposit was given to the guardian with the understanding that his wife and household could also serve as guardians (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 4:8-9), and therefore she too can swear.
he was there. In the victim's house at the time of the robbery.
his hired worker. A temporary worker.

they do not swear and take. For it is doubtful whether they too are considered entrusted with guarding the house, and therefore it is doubtful whether their oath is effective, and money cannot be taken on their word.

and we do not make the robber swear because he is suspect regarding oaths. Since he is established as a robber, he is suspected of swearing a false oath and we do not make him swear (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 2:2).

the homeowner pronounces a general ban. By enactment of the Geonim, in certain cases where a person suspects another of claiming falsely against him and cannot obligate him to an oath, he can impose a ban (curse) in general on anyone who lies against him in that matter without mentioning the suspect's name (see Hilchot Sheluchin ve-Shutafin 3:11, Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:4).

and even if the robber admitted that he robbed part, he returns only the part he admitted. And he is not liable for the oath of one who admits part, since he is liable for it only in a definite claim.
this too is a fine, etc.. Compare Hilchot Mechirah 20:3.
he swears the heset oath like any defendant. See above 5:4 for explanation.
the Torah oath... like anyone who admits part. The oath by the Torah that a defendant is obligated to take when he admitted part of the sum the claimant claimed (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:1).
for he was not established as a robber by witnesses. And therefore he is not suspect regarding the oath.
even though he admitted that he took a pledge without authorization. And transgressed the prohibition of robbery (above 3:16).

since there are no witnesses there... he swears and collects his debt from the pledge. For if there are witnesses that he took it he must return the pledge even if it is known that the borrower owes him (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 3:4).

for the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. Just as the reason to obligate him is based on his statement that he took the vessels, so one can rely on his claim that he took them for his debt in order to exempt him.
as will be explained in Hilchot To'en. 1:2.
and even though this homeowner was accustomed to sell his vessels. And taking out the vessels in itself does not arouse suspicion.

for anyone who enters his fellow's house not in his presence and takes vessels from there... is presumed a robber. And therefore he is not believed even though the manner of taking the vessels is not suspicious (and compare Hilchot Genevah 5:12, where in the opposite situation, when a person took in the presence of the homeowner, he is believed, unless there is a combination of several suspicious circumstances).
and there is no oath here. The homeowner does not need to swear what was taken from him.
and after he returns it he returns and claims, etc.. If he still insists that he took them lawfully, he can sue the homeowner in a separate case.
